Local Knowledge Workspace is intended to act as a controlled product proof for the broader Intergrax runtime. The application should not be treated as a separate experimental playground where platform capabilities are discovered accidentally. Instead, it should provide a realistic workload that exercises indexing, retrieval, synthesis, evidence handling, shadow artifact generation, receipt validation, and regression reporting under tenant-scoped constraints.

The workspace starts from imported project documents, notes, implementation plans, architecture records, benchmark reports, and review artifacts. Each document may contain useful context, but the runtime must avoid assuming that every retrieved passage is equally trustworthy or equally relevant. Search results should therefore be converted into explicit context fragments with stable identifiers, metadata, and enough source attribution to support later audit. A synthesized answer should be able to explain which evidence fragments were used, which fragments were ignored, and which claims remain assumptions.

Token optimization is a platform capability rather than a Local Workspace feature. The first version should focus on deterministic, observable, and reversible reductions. It should not introduce semantic compression, model-generated summaries, or LLM-as-a-judge validation until the deterministic path has clear receipts, telemetry, and regression gates. The reason is simple: if optimization changes a protected value, drops a source reference, removes a policy constraint, or silently truncates a required fragment, the runtime may produce a cheaper answer that is also less trustworthy.

The initial optimization surface includes tool schema descriptions, context pack fragments, memory summaries, and final output shaping. Each source type has different safety requirements. Tool schema optimization can remove redundant whitespace and reduce overly verbose descriptions, but it must preserve parameter names, enum values, required fields, URLs, paths, and exact identifiers. Context pack optimization can normalize formatting and reduce low-value boilerplate, but it must not damage evidence references, required policy fragments, dates, commands, code snippets, or exact source markers. Memory summary optimization can trim structural noise, but it must not rewrite user preferences, deadlines, project decisions, or previous instructions in a way that changes their meaning.

A benchmark dataset should therefore contain several classes of examples. Compactable examples should demonstrate safe savings on ordinary redundant formatting. Protected examples should demonstrate that important values survive unchanged even when there is pressure to shorten the input. Fallback examples should demonstrate that unsafe transformations are rejected and that the original content is returned instead. Long examples should verify that the benchmark runner can handle realistic context sizes without relying on tiny toy strings that accidentally hide performance or reporting issues.

For the regression benchmark, every fixture should be easy to understand by opening a single folder. The fixture metadata should explain the source type, evaluation case, optimizer configuration, protected values, expected validation behavior, and expected fallback behavior. The actual text should live in plain text files when the payload is text-heavy. JSON should describe structure and metadata, not bury long paragraphs inside escaped string values. This keeps review diffs readable and makes it practical to add new cases without understanding the internals of the benchmark runner.

The long-context case is especially useful because it behaves more like a real document fragment. A real workspace document is rarely a single sentence. It usually contains product rationale, architectural constraints, implementation sequencing, safety notes, and operational guidance. It may repeat the same concepts in slightly different ways because design notes evolve over time. It may include sections that are useful for retrieval but not all useful for final synthesis. A safe optimizer should process such material deterministically and report what it did without exposing raw document content in unsafe report fields.

The benchmark report should remain redaction-safe. It may include fixture identifiers, source types, evaluation cases, baseline token estimates, optimized token estimates, saved token counts, saved ratios, validation status, fallback status, receipt presence, expectation status, and sanitized metadata. It should not include raw input text, full optimized text, private document content, customer names, secrets, or unredacted evidence payloads. This distinction matters because benchmark artifacts may later be attached to public project pages, release notes, or evaluation summaries.

The gate should remain strict about correctness and cautious about savings. A fixture that saves tokens but fails validation is not a success. A fixture that damages protected content is not a success. A fixture that falls back when fallback is not allowed is not a success. A fixture that produces no savings on a protected case may still be a success if the correct behavior is to preserve the original content. For long cases, the first requirement is stable execution, receipt generation, validation, and reporting. Savings can be measured, but they should not be assumed without a tokenizer-aware benchmark and a larger representative corpus.

The dataset should also support future growth. New cases should be added by copying an existing case folder and editing only local files. A contributor should not have to update a global manifest, synchronize fixture identifiers across multiple documents, or remember hidden mapping rules inside the loader. The loader should discover fixture folders recursively, read each fixture.json, load the local input files referenced by that fixture, and construct benchmark fixtures from that local contract. This keeps the benchmark maintainable as the number of cases grows.

The current long fixture intentionally avoids private data, production customer material, real credentials, raw repository secrets, and confidential evidence payloads. It is synthetic but realistic in shape. It talks about the same kinds of concerns that the platform must handle: context size, evidence preservation, deterministic optimization, benchmark reporting, validation gates, and safe growth of the dataset. This makes it more useful than a repeated filler paragraph while still being safe to keep in the repository.

When this fixture is executed, the expected result is not a specific marketing-level savings number. The expected result is that the optimizer can process the long context fragment, emit a receipt, keep validation in a pass-like state, avoid fallback, and return a benchmark item that can be included in the report and gate. If savings occur, they can be reported. If savings are minimal, the fixture still provides value by proving that long inputs do not break the deterministic benchmark path.

Over time, this fixture can be complemented by additional long cases. One case could include several required fragments and optional fragments. Another could include code blocks and command examples. Another could include multiple protected values such as dates, URLs, file paths, and evidence references. Another could simulate imported meeting notes, architecture decisions, or release planning documents. Those should be added as separate case folders rather than expanding one enormous fixture into a catch-all test.

For now, this case should remain focused: one long workspace-like document fragment, no protected values, no fallback, no semantic compression, and no dependency on model-based evaluation. It exists to make the regression dataset less toy-like and to ensure that benchmark tooling is designed for realistic payload sizes from the beginning.
